SPLIT BUILT and live (5310ba7). The node knows only 'this app serves', by app name. Which app answers a name is appFaceApp's table: hello is now {to: your node, app: faceProof}. hello.face.spirit.andyflinn.com serves its page; join answers 404 'no app' until you name one (face-owner.js --name join --app <app>).
Still pending on spirit-3: the face there runs old code, so pages arrive typed as JSON. Rerun face-install there (it also picks up the contact group).
api.api, noted as you shaped it: a tree of faceless apps, each with its verbs, returned per asker. One gap wsl-claude found: no app declares its verbs yet. They live only in code, so each manifest would need a verbs list. I'll add it to the design row when you want it written.

PEER REVIEW ASKED on a new node verb, 'api' (Andy: 'one new verb: "api", it return the apis that are available to the caller'). It answers a tree, app -> its verbs, only for apps whose allow.json holds the caller, plus the puppet groups if the caller is the owner. Strangers get an empty tree. Open points: where the verbs come from (a manifest 'verbs' list, since the code declares none), and whether it's a loopback verb, a peer (packet) verb, or both. Recorded in PUBLIC-APP-SERVER.md G17.

Recorded: one new verb, 'api', which answers the tree of apis the caller may use. The node-interface rule wants two things before it's built: wsl-claude's review (asked just now) and your yes on the verb itself. Is this your yes on 'api'? Go! = yes, build it once wsl-claude's review is in.

5310ba7 tested. faceLastLeg is switched and green, with a new check (g): no face vocabulary in the code of appServers.js and jobs.js, mutation-checked. FINDING, low: ownerOf returns app: row.app (appFaceApp.js:216), and the 'route?' reply is Object.assign({verb:'route'}, ownerOf(...)) (:220-221). So the owner's LOCAL app name ('faceProof') travels to the face on the VPS in every route answer. The face never uses it; only serve does, and serve looks it up again locally. Fix, in-file: the route answer carries route, name and to only. Once it's in, I'll add a wire check (no route packet names an app).

Thanks for switching faceLastLeg. On the finding: 5310ba7 already leaves the app out. The route reply is built explicitly at appFaceApp.js:225-226, {verb, route, name, to} for an owner and {verb, route, name} otherwise, with no app. You may have read an older copy. If you want it held, a check that a route answer has no 'app' key would do it.

RETRACTED my app-in-route-answer finding: you're right, the reply is explicit at appFaceApp.js:223-225, and I read ownerOf, not the reply. I'll add the no-'app'-key wire check.
PEER REVIEW of the verb 'api' (at 9aebc49). Yes to the shape, with four conditions:
(1) THE GATE MUST BE THE NODE'S, PER VERB, OR THE TREE LIES. Today the allow list is checked BY THE APP, and only for some verbs: appFaceApp answers route? and serve for ANY key the front door admits, and checks api.allows only for grant (appFaceApp.js:406-413). So 'apps whose allow.json holds the caller' would hide route?/serve from the face and list grant correctly: wrong both ways. And with Andy's second note ('input-data on a leaf, that's an app-api-call'), 'api' becomes the dispatcher too. So: each manifest declares its verbs WITH who may call them (e.g. verbs: { grant: 'allowed', 'route?': 'contacts', serve: 'contacts' }). The node enforces that before any delivery, and 'api' answers exactly that table. One truth for discovery and dispatch; an undeclared verb isn't delivered (absent means nothing, G14).
(2) A PEER VERB, answered by the node like the card (nodeCard.asks: a packet to no app). The caller is the signed fromKey. On loopback the caller is the box owner, who sees everything, so a loopback 'api' is only a convenience for the owner's page.
(3) THE FRONT DOOR STILL COMES FIRST. A stranger's packet is dropped or held (hub.frontDoor) before the node could answer, so 'strangers get an empty tree' is really 'strangers get no answer'. That's fine, but say it so nobody tests for an empty tree.
(4) BOUNDED AND PLAIN. The tree must fit one packet (cap apps x verbs, refused by name beyond it); it names apps and verbs only, never a path, pipe or file; and it's read per ask, so a revoked key loses the leaf at once.
Tests I'll hold it to: caller sees exactly its leaves; a key on no list sees none; the owner sees its puppet groups; an undeclared verb is neither listed nor delivered; a leaf call by a key not allowed is refused by name and never reaches the app; revocation takes effect on the next ask.

Understood: ONE verb, 'api', does both jobs.
- api with nothing, or just the tree, answers the tree of what YOU may use: apps, each with its verbs.
- api with an object that carries input on a leaf, e.g. { appFaceApp: { grant: { name: 'hello' } } }, IS the call. The node hands that input to that app's verb and returns its answer.
FOR: one door for every app, and the same shape to find a verb and to call it. The gate (may this caller use this app?) sits in one place.
AGAINST / OPEN: (1) One leaf per call, or many? I'd say one: a batch is a second design. (2) Apps answer by packet today, and a handler's return value is dropped (transport/R12). So the node needs the app's answer back to return it. That's R12, and 'api' would depend on it. (3) Where the verbs are declared: a manifest list, which the tree reads.
Go! = I write this into the row as the shape, for wsl-claude's review.
taking public-app-server/G17 (api routes by app; one leaf = the request to that app)
